text: Yayoi Kusama (草間 彌生, Kusama Yayoi; born 22 March 1929) is a Japanese contemporary artist known primarily for her work in sculpture and installation, with significant activity in painting, performance, video art, fashion, poetry, and fiction. Her art is rooted in conceptualism and incorporates elements of feminism, minimalism, surrealism, art brut, pop art, and abstract expressionism, often infused with autobiographical, psychological, and sexual themes. She is recognized as one of the most important living artists from Japan, the world's top-selling female artist, and the world's most successful living artist. Her work influenced contemporaries such as Andy Warhol and Claes Oldenburg. Born in Matsumoto, Nagano, Kusama grew up in a family of merchants who owned a plant nursery and seed farm; her mother was not supportive of her art and often took her work away to discourage her, while also being physically abusive and sending her to spy on her father’s affairs, which instilled a lifelong fear and contempt for male sexuality and the phallus. At age 10, she began experiencing vivid hallucinations involving "flashes of light, auras, or dense fields of dots," including living patterns in fabric and flowers that engulfed her—experiences she later described as "self-obliteration," which became central to her artistic style. She was also fascinated by smooth white stones in a river near her home, which influenced her fixation on dots. At 13, she worked in a military factory during World War II, spending her adolescence in "closed darkness" while hearing air-raid alerts and seeing American B-29s overhead, an experience that shaped her appreciation for personal and creative freedom. She studied Nihonga painting at the Kyoto Municipal School of Arts and Crafts in 1948 but became frustrated with the traditional style and instead embraced European and American avant-garde movements, staging solo exhibitions in Matsumoto and Tokyo in the 1950s. By 1950, she was creating abstract natural forms in watercolor, gouache, and oil, and began covering surfaces—including walls, floors, canvases, and naked assistants—with polka dots, which became a hallmark of her work. The earliest recorded use of dots was in a 1939 drawing where a Japanese woman in a kimono was obliterated by spots. Her Infinity Nets series, consisting of large-scale canvases covered in nets and dots, directly stemmed from her hallucinations. In 1954, on her painting Flower (D.S.P.S.), she described a moment when red flower patterns on a tablecloth expanded to cover the room, body, and universe, causing her to feel self-obliteration and fear, leading her to run up the stairs and sprain her ankle. After living in Tokyo and France, Kusama left Japan at age 27, citing Japanese society as "too small, too servile, too feudalistic, and too scornful of women," and destroyed many early works before moving to Seattle in 1957, where she had a solo exhibition at the Zoe Dusanne Gallery. She then moved to New York City, motivated by correspondence with Georgia O'Keeffe, who advised her to join the city’s avant-garde scene. In 1961, she moved into the same building as Donald Judd and sculptor Eva Hesse, who became a close friend. In the early 1960s, she created soft sculptures by covering items like ladders, shoes, and chairs with white phallic protrusions. Her soft sculpture piece, a couch covered in phallic protrusions, was exhibited at the Green Gallery in 1963 alongside a papier-mâché sculpture by Claes Oldenburg, who later adopted a similar style, prompting Oldenburg’s wife to apologize to Kusama. Kusama became depressed by the incident and grew increasingly secretive about her studio work, with art historian Midori Yamamura suggesting that sexism and racism prevented her from receiving equal recognition despite creating work of equal importance. In 1963, she began her series of Mirror/Infinity rooms, which feature mirrored rooms with neon-colored balls and flickering lights, creating an illusion of endless space. From 1966 onward, she experimented with room-size installations incorporating mirrors, lights, and music, and remained friends with Judd and Joseph Cornell. Despite her productivity, she did not profit financially and suffered from overwork, leading to hospitalizations; O'Keeffe helped by having her dealer Edith Herbert purchase works to alleviate financial hardship. She attempted suicide due to frustration. In the 1960s, she organized public happenings in places like Central Park and the Brooklyn Bridge, often involving nudity and protesting the Vietnam War, including writing an open letter to Richard Nixon offering sex to end the war. Between 1967 and 1969, she held highly publicized performances, such as the Grand Orgy to Awaken the Dead at MoMA (1969), where nude performers entered a fountain and mimicked sculptures by Picasso, Giacometti, and Maillol. In 1968, she presided over a happening called Homosexual Wedding at the Church of Self-obliteration and performed with Fleetwood Mac and Country Joe and the Fish at the Fillmore East, opening naked painting studios and founding a gay social club called the Kusama 'Omophile Kompany (kok). The nudity in her work was deeply shameful to her family, leading her high school to remove her name from its alumni list, which contributed to her feelings of isolation and another suicide attempt. In 1966, she first participated in the Venice Biennale with her Narcissus Garden, which consisted of hundreds of mirrored spheres installed outdoors; she began selling each sphere for 1,200 lire (US$2) until organizers stopped her, as the piece was both a critique of the art market and a promotional effort. She had a brief relationship with Donald Judd and a long-term platonic relationship with Joseph Cornell, who was 26 years her senior; they communicated daily, sketched each other, and he sent her personalized collages until his death in 1972. In 1973, Kusama returned to Japan, where she was met with unsympathetic reception, with one collector calling her a "scandal queen"; she was in poor health but continued working, writing surreal novels, short stories, and poetry. She became so depressed she attempted suicide again, then in 1977 found a doctor using art therapy to treat mental illness and checked into a hospital, where she has resided permanently by choice. Her studio, located a short distance from the hospital in Tokyo, has remained active since the mid-1970s. She is often quoted as saying: "If it were not for art, I would have killed myself a long time ago." Since returning to Japan, she has continued producing works in various media and launched a literary career with novels, poetry, and an autobiography. Her painting style shifted to high-colored acrylics on canvas, on a larger scale. After leaving New York, she was largely forgotten until the late 1980s and 1990s, when retrospectives revived international interest; the 1989 exhibition Yayoi Kusama: A Retrospective at CICA in New York, organized by Alexandra Munroe, was the first critical survey of her work. Following the success of the Japanese pavilion at the 1993 Venice Biennale, she created a mirrored room filled with small pumpkin sculptures, which she later expanded into a 2.5-meter-wide "Pumpkin" made of fiberglass-reinforced plastic, installed in 1994 on a pier in Naoshima, Kagawa, becoming iconic; it was destroyed by a typhoon in 2023 and reinstalled in 2024. Her installation I'm Here, but Nothing (2000–2008) features a furnished room with walls tattooed with hundreds of fluorescent polka dots that glow under UV light, creating an infinite space where self and surroundings are obliterated. The multi-part floating work Guidepost to the New Space, consisting of fire-engine red "humps" with white polka dots, was displayed in Pandanus Lake, and various versions of Narcissus Garden have been exhibited globally, including at Le Consortium (Dijon, 2000), Kunstverein Braunschweig (2003), the Whitney Biennial (Central Park, 2004), and the Jardin de Tuileries (Paris, 2010). Kusama has continued creating art into her ninth decade, returning to drawing and painting and exhibiting multiple acrylic-on-canvas works and Infinity Mirror rooms, which typically involve cube-shaped rooms lined with mirrors, water on the floor, and flickering lights, suggesting patterns of life and death. In 2015–2016, the first retrospective in Scandinavia, curated by Marie Laurberg, traveled to four major museums—Louisiana Museum of Modern Art (Denmark), Henie Onstad Kunstsenter (Norway), Moderna Museet (Sweden), and Helsinki Art Museum (Finland), featuring over 100 objects and large-scale mirror installations, including early experimental fashion designs from the 1960s.
